title: 188 Relationship of yearling Angus bull pulmonary arterial pressure estimates with production, maternal, and carcass Expected Progeny Differences (EPDs)
content:
Abstract
Pulmonary arterial pressure (PAP) determines an animal’s susceptibility to High Altitude Disease (HAD), which causes pulmonary hypertension due to hypoxia. It is estimated that 1.5 million head of cattle are raised in high altitude environments (above 1,500 m) and HAD accounts for 3-5% of calf death loss yearly. The objectives of this study were to model the relationship of PAP estimates with production, maternal, and carcass expected progeny differences (EPDs). Bull PAP estimates were collected from Angus yearling bulls ranging in age from 12 – 18-month-old from a Montana-based Angus operation (> 1,600 m elevation, 5,400 yearlings/18-month-old bulls from 2016 – 2023). We used Akaike’s Information Criterion adjusted for small sample sizes (AICc) to evaluate support for competing models reflecting hypotheses about the effects of bull age at time of testing and performance EPDs. Models containing an asymptotic relationship between PAP and all measured variables were the best supported from the candidate model sets for all but the calving ease direct model which was best supported by a linear relationship. Bull age at time of testing was supported in most model selection for the EPDs measured. Bulls with greater calving ease direct had lower PAP scores (P < 0.01; Fall Sale: β = -0.06 ± 0.02; Spring Sale: β = -0.15 ± 0.03; R2marginal = 0.62 %; R2conditional = 1.06 %). In addition, bulls with higher birth weight EPDs had higher PAP estimates (P < 0.01; Fall Sale: β = 1.87 ± 0.32; Spring Sale: β = 1.68 ± 0.32; R2marginal = 0.73 %; R2conditional = 1.15 %). Pulmonary arterial pressure was greater for bulls that had greater weaning weight EPDs (P < 0.01; Fall Sale: β = 1.87 ± 0.32; Spring Sale: β = 1.68 ± 0.32; R2marginal = 0.73 %; R2conditional = 1.15 %) and for bulls that had greater yearling weight EPDs (P < 0.01; β = 2.29 ± 0.71; R2marginal = 0.24 %; R2conditional = 0.93%). There were no observed relationships between bull PAP and scrotal circumference EPDs (P = 0.28) and maternal milk EPDs (P = 0.51). Bulls with greater PAP had greater carcass weight EPDs (P =0.03; Fall Sale: β = 0.77 ± 0.35; Spring Sale: β = 0.65 ± 0.35; R2marginal = 0.17 %; R2conditional = 0.69 %). There were no observed relationships between bull PAP and ribeye area EPDs (P = 0.17) and marbling EPDs (P = 0.21). Dam sire lines with greater than 100 yearling bulls tended to differ (P=0.09) and, from the highest to lowest ranged 2.1 mmHg. In summary, PAP was related to calving ease direct, birth weight, weaning weight, yearling weight, and carcass weight EPDs. However, these relationships explain very little of the variation of PAP estimates.
